summary: NFSv4 lets a client open a file and also receive a delegation, which gives it the right to cache information about that file locally. This RFC adds several extensions to NFSv4.2 for opening files and delegating them to clients, making those operations more flexible and efficient.

eli5.summary: When you borrow a book from a library, the librarian may let you keep it a while without checking in. This adds smarter ways to borrow files on a network and keep a local copy.

questions: how to open and delegate a file in nfs
what is open xor delegation in nfs
how does nfsv4 offline attribute work
subtitle: Four NFSv4.2 extensions that let clients spot offline files, skip a CLOSE, and cache file times under a delegation.

tldr.problem: NFSv4.2 clients cannot tell if a file is offline, cannot discover which OPEN features a server supports, pay for extra CLOSE and DELEGRETURN round trips, and cannot hand access and modify times back to the server while holding a delegation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an offline attribute, a fattr4_open_arguments attribute for feature discovery, an OPEN flag that returns either an open or a delegation stateid, and a flag plus two attributes that let a delegation holder proxy access and modify times.
tldr.outcome: Clients avoid needless file retrievals and server queries, and the typical create-and-write workload needs fewer synchronous operations.

today: RFC 9754 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2025, and the unit metadata shows it has not been obsoleted or updated. It extends NFSv4.2 as described in RFC 7862.

sections.title: What the Extensions Add
sections.content:
In NFSv4 a client may be granted a delegation for a file, which lets it act as the authority for the file's data and metadata. This document adds extensions that let the client:

  • detect an offline file, which may require significant effort to obtain;
  • determine which extensions of OPEN flags the server supports;
  • retrieve either the open or the delegation stateid, but not both, during OPEN; and
  • cache both the access and modify timestamps, so it queries the server less often.

Following the process in RFC 8178, these revisions become an extension of NFSv4.2 (RFC 7862). They build on the XDR generated from RFC 7863. The XDR for the new items is embedded in the document and can be pulled out with a short shell script.
sections.eli5: The library adds four new rules: knowing if a book is in the warehouse, knowing which borrowing options exist, borrowing with less paperwork, and keeping your own reading dates.

sections.title: Offline Files
sections.content:
An offline file sits on a device not connected to the server. Bringing it online usually costs something: historically, finding and loading a tape; more recently, a monetary charge to download from the cloud. The server has fast access to the file's attributes but not to its contents.

A compound with GETATTR or READDIR can report attributes without bringing the file online, but an OPEN or a LAYOUTGET might make the server retrieve the data. A file manager that previews a file as a user hovers over it could trigger that retrieval by mistake.

The new attribute fattr4_offline (a boolean, attribute number 83) lets a client check availability first and avoid opening the file at all.
sections.eli5: Some books are kept in a far-away warehouse and fetching one costs money. A new sign on the shelf tells you the book is in the warehouse, so you do not ask for it just to peek.

sections.title: Discovering OPEN Features
sections.content:
Section 4.4.2 of RFC 8178 allows extending a minor version without defining a new one, with the client probing the server's capabilities. The new fattr4_open_arguments attribute (number 86) supports this. It models all OPEN parameters as bitmap4 fields, so a flag can be added to any of them, and its scope covers all objects with a matching fsid.

Two new flags use it: OPEN4_SHARE_ACCESS_WANT_OPEN_XOR_DELEGATION and OPEN4_SHARE_ACCESS_WANT_DELEG_TIMESTAMPS. Future OPTIONAL OPEN features can add a flag each.

Because fattr4_open_arguments is a RECOMMENDED attribute, if the server answers NFS4ERR_ATTRNOTSUPP the client MUST take that to mean the new OPTIONAL OPEN functionality is not supported. The server MUST mark REQUIRED flags as supported, and flags MUST only change from OPTIONAL to REQUIRED when the NFSv4 minor version is incremented.
sections.eli5: Before ordering, you ask the librarian for the menu of what you may ask for. If there is no menu, you assume the fancy options are not offered.

sections.title: Open or Delegation Stateid
sections.content:
OPEN returns an open stateid, and the client may also ask for a delegation stateid. A file counts as open for the client as long as the count of open and delegated stateids is greater than 0, and either kind lets READ, WRITE, LOCK and LAYOUTGET proceed. If the client gets both, it has to return both.

If the client knows the server supports OPEN4_SHARE_ACCESS_WANT_OPEN_XOR_DELEGATION, it can set it in OPEN and get either an open or a delegation stateid. If the server sends no open stateid it MUST set the result flag OPEN4_RESULT_NO_OPEN_STATEID and MUST set OPEN4resok.stateid to the special all-zero stateid.

The flag is only a hint, and the server might return both. For example, a client first opens read-only and gets only an open stateid, then opens read-write; the server may return only an open stateid, only a delegation stateid (with the open stateid now needing an upgrade), or both. Returning just a delegation stateid would hide information from a client that already holds an open stateid, so in that case the server SHOULD ignore the flag and return both.
sections.eli5: When you borrow a book you can get a library card or a permission slip. Usually you get just one so there is less to give back, but if you already have a card, the librarian gives you both.

sections.title: Implementation Experience
sections.content:
CLOSE neither explicitly nor implicitly releases any delegation stateids, unlike OPEN, which can grant both. The authors say they could have extended CLOSE to release both, but implementation experience shows that is more costly than the chosen approach.

Take the workload of creating a file with content. Existing implementations use three synchronous operations (OPEN, WRITE, CLOSE) and one asynchronous operation (DELEGRETURN). With the OPEN_XOR_DELEGATION flag, the client no longer needs to send CLOSE and can delay DELEGRETURN until the server recalls the delegation or garbage collection causes the client to return it.

The RFC states this reduces the cost of synchronous operations by 33% and the total number of operations by 25%. Having CLOSE return both stateids would not reduce the number of synchronous operations.
sections.eli5: Instead of three trips to the desk, you make two, and you hand back the permission slip later when it is convenient.

sections.title: Proxying of Times
sections.content:
A client with a write delegation is the authority for the file's contents and attributes, but under unextended NFSv4 a server using CB_GETATTR can learn only the size and the change attribute. Setting the times with SETATTR before DELEGRETURN would alter the change or time_metadata attributes on the server, so the server cannot give POSIX-compliant times to applications.

With the OPEN4_SHARE_ACCESS_WANT_DELEG_TIMESTAMPS flag, the client becomes the authority for the access and modify times and passes them back at DELEGRETURN. Two attributes carry them, fattr4_time_deleg_access (84) and fattr4_time_deleg_modify (85). If a server advertises support and returns a valid delegation for such an OPEN, it MUST query the client with CB_GETATTR for both. On SETATTR it MUST accept the values or reject them with NFS4ERR_DELAY. The server MUST set OPEN_DELEGATE_READ_ATTRS_DELEG or OPEN_DELEGATE_WRITE_ATTRS_DELEG to show which delegation it granted.

These attributes are invalid with GETATTR, VERIFY and NVERIFY. The SETATTR SHOULD be in a separate compound before the DELEGRETURN or earlier in the same compound, or race conditions may arise.

Client and server clocks must be in sync. The server compares each presented time to the file's existing time and the current server time. A time before the original is ignored. A time in the future can be clamped to the current time or answered with NFS4ERR_DELAY, which with large skew can deny access until the skew has passed. A change in access time MUST NOT advance the change time. A modify time between the change time and now moves the change time to the modify time. All comparisons should use the same current-time value.

The RFC also gives a use case: an NFSv3 server acting as an NFSv4.2 client gateway can proxy delegations and answer attribute queries without sending GETATTR to the NFSv4.2 server.
sections.eli5: If you hold a book, you know when you last read and wrote in it. The new rules let you tell the library those dates when you return it, as long as your watch matches the library's clock.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says there are no new security concerns. Other clients cannot query the client about cached attributes, and a client could already report false data through a SETATTR operation. IANA has no actions to take.
sections.eli5: Nothing new can go wrong that could not already go wrong, so there are no new safety rules.
